problem_data.story:
Dr. Sophia Edwards left her laboratory at the Oceanographic Research Institute in Oakdale Village at exactly 6:00 PM and began the evening walk she had taken, without fail, for fifteen solid years.

The walk never varied. She paced three blocks down Harbor Street, stopped at the Blue Whale Café to purchase a kelp tea, then walked to the end of the fifth block on Harbor. There she turned left on Maritime Avenue, followed Maritime to Coral Street, down Coral and so by way of Beacon back to Harbor again and to her small apartment above the institute.

She didn't walk quickly. She took her time. She always returned to her door at exactly 6:50 PM. No one ever stopped to talk with her. Even the barista at the Blue Whale Café remained silent while preparing her drink. Dr. Edwards merely nodded, the woman prepared the tea, and Dr. Edwards took her cup. That was all.

For people long ago had gathered that Dr. Edwards desired solitude. The newer generation of researchers called it dedication to her work. Certain colleagues had a different word for it. The senior scientists remembered that this intense woman with her waterproof notebook, titanium data collection tools, and ever-present rain jacket had once been a celebrated professor at Ravenswood Regional University.

The notebook was her constant companion—she was never without it. In fifteen years, no colleague had ever seen Dr. Edwards separated from that waterproof notebook, not for a single moment during working hours. She carried it everywhere: to the laboratory, on her walks, even clutching it during the rare institute-wide safety drills. The notebook contained her observations, her measurements, her meticulous records of oceanic phenomena spanning a decade and a half.

A professor of oceanography, they recalled, specializing in deep-sea ecosystems and marine resource management. At any rate, a controversy of some sort was connected with her name—an academic dispute. She had published a research paper, and she had presented that research to international conferences. What that research proposed had long been forgotten by most, but whatever it was had been considered sufficiently radical to cost Dr. Edwards her tenured position at the university.

A pale moon hung over the harbor and a sharp, salt-tinged wind was blowing when Dr. Edwards started out at six o'clock.

It was a good evening, she told herself, breathing the clean ocean air and the faint scent of seaweed from the nearby docks.

She walked steadily, her notebook tucked securely in her jacket pocket—its familiar weight against her side, the one possession she would never leave behind. She noticed that the streetlight at the corner of Harbor and Beacon was flickering, and she frowned slightly when forced to step around construction barriers before the entrance to Building 47.

It seemed she reached the corner of Maritime and Harbor just a bit too quickly, but she told herself this couldn't be. For fifteen years, since the year following her dismissal from the university, she had lived by precise routine.

The same thing, at the same time, day after day. She had not deliberately chosen such a regimented existence. A single woman, living alone with her research stipend and savings, the timed routine had developed gradually—a framework for maintaining work-life balance in the absence of other anchors.

So she turned on Maritime and back on Coral. The security guard at the corner of Coral and Beacon nodded to her as always, a silent acknowledgment of her nightly passage.

A news broadcast was playing from someone's open window, and fragments drifted to Dr. Edwards.

"...continuing to occur worldwide...entire research station in Larchmont Province vanished...leading marine biologist, Dr. Christopher Lane, cannot explain..."

The wind carried the words away and Dr. Edwards pressed her lips together. Another sensationalist report, probably. She remembered similar panic years before, something about atmospheric anomalies. And Lane! What did Lane have to do with anything? He was one of the scientists who had dismissed her paper as pseudoscience.

But she pushed the thought away, focused on the familiar rhythm of her steps, looked at the known landmarks that emerged from the coastal darkness as she walked. For there was nothing—absolutely nothing in the world—that she would let disturb her equilibrium. That was a principle she had established fifteen years ago.

There was a group of researchers outside the institute's main entrance at the corner of Coral and Beacon, talking urgently. Dr. Edwards caught excited phrases: "It's happening in every coastal region...What could cause this...The data analysis shows nothing..."

But as Dr. Edwards approached, they fell silent and watched her pass. She, for her part, gave them no acknowledgment. That was how it had been for many years, ever since people had accepted that she did not wish to engage.

One of the researchers, a young woman named Camila Bryant, half-stepped forward as if to speak, but then retreated, and Dr. Edwards continued her walk.

Back at her apartment door, she stopped and, as she had done a thousand times before, checked her waterproof watch.

She stared at it in confusion. It was only 6:35 PM.

For long minutes she stood examining the watch. The timepiece hadn't stopped; its second hand still swept smoothly around the face.

But fifteen minutes too early! For fifteen years, day in and day out, she had left at six and returned at ten minutes to seven. Now...

It wasn't until then that she realized something else was wrong. She had no kelp tea. For the first time, she had failed to stop at the Blue Whale Café.

Shaken, muttering to herself, Dr. Edwards unlocked her apartment and secured the door behind her.

She hung her jacket on the hook in the entryway—then paused, reaching back to retrieve the notebook from the pocket. She would not leave it there, even overnight, even in her own home. She carried it with her into the living area.

Dropping into her reading chair, she set the notebook on the side table and shook her head in bewilderment. Her eyes drifted automatically to the wall opposite, finding the familiar image there—the underwater scene she had positioned directly in her line of sight when she'd first arranged this room, so she could see it without turning her head.

Silence filled the room. A silence measured by the soft hum of the temperature control system.

But silence was familiar to Dr. Edwards. Once she had enjoyed music—classical recordings she could stream through her speakers. But the speakers sat disconnected in the corner. Dr. Edwards had unplugged them years before, precisely on the evening when a concert had been interrupted for breaking news.

She had stopped following news feeds and scientific journals too, had isolated herself to a few city blocks. And as the years passed, that self-imposed isolation had become absolute, an invisible but impenetrable boundary marking an area five blocks by four. Beyond that perimeter lay something she could not name, would not acknowledge. Beyond it, she never ventured.

But recluse though she was, she could not entirely escape information. Things researchers discussed in the hallways, fragments of broadcasts from open windows, headlines glimpsed on discarded tablets.

And so she knew this was the year 2089, and that the conflicts in the Pacific territories and Asian coastal regions had ended in catastrophe, followed by a mysterious phenomenon—a plague of disappearances sweeping through region after region like an invisible tide, erasing populations. A phenomenon undoubtedly connected to the wars and their disruption of natural resource management systems.

But those things she dismissed as concerns far removed from her small world. She disregarded them. She pretended she had never heard of them. Others might worry and theorize if they wished. To her, they simply did not matter.

But there were two things tonight that did matter. Two disturbing, inexplicable events. She had arrived home fifteen minutes early. She had forgotten her kelp tea.

Huddled in the chair, she frowned. It was unsettling to have her routine disrupted. There must be something wrong. Had her long isolation finally affected her mind—perhaps just slightly—enough to impair her judgment? Had she lost her sense of temporal precision, of spatial awareness?

No, she hadn't. Take this room, for example. After fifteen years, it had become as integral to her identity as her research methodology. Every detail was recorded in her mind with scientific clarity: the titanium desk with its organized specimen samples; the shelf with her carefully maintained equipment; the chronometer that displayed not only time but date, lunar phase, and tidal information; the specimen jar on the side table; her waterproof notebook beside it; and on the wall, the framed photograph.

The photograph showed an underwater scene in the foreground, a coral reef teeming with life. Far in the distance, almost at the edge of visibility, was the vague outline of a research submersible. Dr. Edwards had acquired it during her years at the university, before her dismissal—a memento of fieldwork in the Pacific, of a time when she had believed her research would change the world.

There were other images too. The coastal landscape above the storage unit, the marine charts in the corner where she sat, the satellite imagery above the bookshelf. But the reef photograph hung on the wall directly facing her chair. When she sat here in the evenings, her eyes found it naturally, inevitably. It was the first thing she saw upon sitting, the last thing she looked at before rising.

Further reflection became difficult as Dr. Edwards felt exhaustion overtaking her. She prepared for bed mechanically, slipping the notebook into the drawer of her bedside table where it remained each night. For an hour she lay awake, troubled by undefined anxieties she could neither articulate nor comprehend.

When finally she slept, it was to experience a series of disturbing dreams. She dreamed first that she was conducting fieldwork on a small research platform in the open ocean, that the waters around the platform teemed with unknown organisms—bioluminescent creatures that pulsed with alien light—and that steadily those organisms were consuming the platform itself.

In another dream, she was pursued by something she could neither observe nor measure, but only sense. And as she tried to flee, she remained stationary. Her legs moved frantically, but she made no progress. It was as if she ran on a treadmill in the laboratory.

Then again the threat surrounded her, a vast, incomprehensible presence, and she tried to call out but couldn't. She opened her mouth and strained but filled her lungs to bursting with the effort to shout—but no sound emerged.

All next day she was uneasy, and as she left the apartment that evening at precisely 6:00 PM, she kept reminding herself: "You must not forget tonight! You must remember to stop for your tea!"

She patted her jacket pocket, confirming the notebook's presence—a reassuring ritual she performed dozens of times daily. The notebook was essential to her work, irreplaceable. Without it, she would feel exposed, vulnerable.

The streetlight at the corner of Beacon was still flickering, and in front of Building 47 the construction barriers remained in place. Everything appeared the same as the night before.

And now, she told herself, the Blue Whale Café is in the next block. I must not forget tonight. To forget twice consecutively would be unacceptable.

She held that thought firmly in mind, walked just slightly faster down the street.

But at the corner she stopped, disoriented. Bewildered, she stared down the next block. There was no blue neon sign, no welcoming light on the sidewalk to mark the small café tucked into this research district.

She stared at the street marker and read the word slowly: MARITIME. She read it again, disbelieving, for this shouldn't be Maritime Avenue, but Dock Street. She had walked two blocks, and the café was between Dock and Maritime. She hadn't reached Dock yet—and here was Maritime.

Or had she, absent-mindedly, walked one block farther than intended, passed the café as on the previous night?

For the first time in fifteen years, Dr. Edwards retraced her steps. She walked back to Beacon, then turned and went back to Maritime again and on to Coral. Then back to Maritime again, where she stood stunned while a single, impossible fact crystallized in her mind:

There wasn't any café! The block from Dock to Maritime had disappeared!

Now she understood why she had missed the café the night before, why she had arrived home fifteen minutes early.

On legs that felt numb, she stumbled back to her apartment. She locked the door behind her and made her way unsteadily to her chair in the corner.

What was this? What did it mean? By what inconceivable mechanism could a paved street with buildings, equipment, and structures be erased and the space it had occupied be closed up?

Was something happening in the world that she, in her isolated existence, knew nothing about?

Dr. Edwards shivered, started to adjust her jacket, then stopped as she realized the room temperature was regulated. The cold she felt came from somewhere else. The cold of fear and uncertainty, the chill of half-formed understanding.

Her eyes found the reef photograph on the wall—the coral formations, the distant submersible, the blue depths she had once explored. Looking at it steadied her somehow, as it always did.

A profound silence had descended, a silence still measured by the chronometer's digital display. And yet a silence that held a different quality than she had ever experienced before. Not a comfortable, familiar silence—but a silence that suggested emptiness and void.

There was something behind this, Dr. Edwards told herself. Something that connected to fragments of memory buried in her consciousness, demanding recognition. Something tied to the conversations she had overheard at the institute, pieces of broadcasts she had heard while walking, the urgent discussions among researchers. Something related to events in the world from which she had withdrawn.

She recalled them now and focused on the central theme: the wars and disappearances. Hints of Pacific territories and Asian coastal regions swept nearly clean of human presence, of the phenomenon spreading through African coastlines, of its appearance in South American ports, of the desperate efforts of North American authorities to prevent its advance.

Millions of people had vanished from Pacific and Asian regions, African and South American coasts. Billions, perhaps.

And somehow those grim statistics seemed connected to her own experience. Something, somewhere, some element of her earlier research, seemed to hold an explanation. But try as she might, her confused mind failed to find the answer.

The chronometer advanced silently, its display shifting from 7:29 to 7:30.

Dr. Edwards stood, walked to the window, and looked out.

Moonlight painted the harbor in silver and black, silhouetting the cranes and vessels against a luminous sky.

But the research building directly across the street was not the same. It was strangely distorted, its proportions wrong, like a structure that had suddenly become non-Euclidean.

She stared at it in shock, trying to determine what was wrong. She recalled how it had always stood, solid, a standard example of modern marine research architecture.

Then, before her eyes, the building corrected itself. Slowly it resolved, smoothed out its strange angles, readjusted its dimensions, became once again the familiar structure she knew it must be.

With relief, Dr. Edwards turned back toward the room.

But before she moved away from the window, she looked again. The building was distorted—as severe, perhaps worse than before!

Gasping, Dr. Edwards moved away from the window, went to her bedroom, and took sedatives from her medical kit.

Her dreams that night were the same as before. Again there was the research platform in open ocean. Again she was alone upon it. Again the bioluminescent organisms were consuming her foundation piece by piece.

She woke, body drenched with perspiration. Dim light of early dawn filtered through the window. The clock beside her bed showed 7:15 AM. For a long time she lay motionless.

Again the inexplicable events of the night before returned to haunt her, and as she lay there staring at the window, she remembered them one by one. But her mind, still clouded by sleep and confusion, processed the events mechanically, lost the sharp edge of terror that surrounded them.

The light through the window slowly brightened. Dr. Edwards slid out of bed, crossed to the window, the cold floor against her bare feet. She forced herself to look out.

There was nothing outside the window. No shapes. As if there might be fog. But no fog, however dense, could obscure the equipment storage shed that stood close to the building.

But the shed was there—shadowy, indistinct in the gray light, with rust visible on its panels, a few identification markers still attached to its surface.

The shed was there now. But it hadn't been when she first looked. Dr. Edwards was certain of that.

And now she saw the faint outline of the adjacent research building—but that outline was wrong. The dimensions didn't align properly—they were distorted. As if some massive force had grasped the building and twisted it out of true. Like the building she had seen across the street the night before, the building that had painfully corrected itself when she focused on how it should appear.

Perhaps if she concentrated on how the adjacent building should look, it too might correct itself. But Dr. Edwards was exhausted. Too exhausted to focus on the building.

She turned from the window and dressed slowly. In the living area, she collapsed into her chair, rested her feet on the ottoman. For a long time she sat, trying to think. Her gaze kept drifting to the reef photograph, the coral formations offering a strange comfort—a reminder of a world that had once made sense.

And then, abruptly, something like an electrical shock ran through her. Rigid, she sat there, hollow inside at the realization. Minutes later she rose and almost ran across the room to the bookshelf mounted on the wall.

There were many volumes on the shelf: her reference texts on the first level, her research journals on the lower levels. The second level contained but one publication. And it was around this publication that Dr. Edwards' entire professional life had revolved.

Fifteen years ago she had written it and foolishly attempted to present its hypothesis to the international oceanographic community. The media, she remembered, had sensationalized it extensively. Controversy had erupted. Narrow-minded colleagues, failing to understand either her methodology or her conclusions, but seeing in her another proponent of pseudoscience, had forced her resignation from the university.

It was a straightforward paper, really, dismissed by most authorities as merely the speculation of an overzealous researcher.

Dr. Edwards took it down now, opened the cover, and began reading slowly through the pages. For a moment, the memory of her former career swept over her.

Then her eyes focused on a paragraph, a paragraph written so long ago the very words seemed foreign and distant:

"Human consciousness itself, through collective observation and measurement, maintains the physical structure of observable reality—yes, even the ocean depths we study. Billions of minds perceiving currents as currents, organisms as organisms, geological formations as formations—and not as something else. Minds that observe phenomena as they are and have maintained phenomena as they were. Eliminate those minds, and the entire framework of matter, deprived of its observational foundation, will collapse and transform like a column of sand..."

Her eyes followed down the page:

"Yet this would relate not to matter itself—but only to matter's configuration. For while human consciousness through long ages may have shaped our understanding of the space we inhabit, consciousness would have limited conceivable influence upon the existence of that matter. What exists in our known universe shall exist perpetually and can never be destroyed, only altered or transformed.

"But in modern theoretical physics and oceanography, we gain insight into the possibility—yes, probability—that there are other dimensions, other frameworks of space-time intersecting with the one we occupy.

"If a probe is inserted into a two-dimensional plane, would that plane have any knowledge of the probe? It would not, for in this case the plane is two-dimensional, the probe three-dimensional. Yet both occupy the same space.

"Granting then that the power of human consciousness alone maintains this universe, or at least this world in its present configuration, may we not go further and envision other consciousnesses in some other dimension observing us, waiting, waiting strategically for the moment they can assume control of matter? Such a concept is not impossible. It is a logical conclusion if we accept the dual hypothesis: that consciousness does control the configuration of all matter; and that other realities exist in juxtaposition with ours.

"Perhaps we shall encounter a day, far distant, when our dimension, our world will dissolve beneath our feet and before our eyes as some stronger consciousness reaches out from the dimensional shadows of the very space we inhabit and wrests from us the matter which we know to be our own."

She stood stunned beside the bookshelf, her eyes staring unseeing at the window.

She had written that. And because of those words, she had been called a pseudoscientist, had been compelled to resign her position at the university, had been forced into this isolated existence.

A tremendous realization struck her. Humans had vanished by the millions worldwide. Where there had been thousands of minds, there now were one or two. An insufficient force to maintain the configuration of matter intact.

The disappearances had swept Pacific and Asian regions nearly clean of life, had devastated African coasts, had reached South American ports—might even have come to North America. She remembered the whispers she had heard, the words of the researchers at the institute entrance, the buildings vanishing. Something scientists could not explain. But those were merely fragments of information. She did not know the complete picture—she could not know. She never monitored broadcasts, never read scientific journals.

But abruptly everything fit together in her mind like the solution to a complex equation. The significance of it all gripped her with devastating clarity.

There were not sufficient consciousnesses in existence to maintain the material world in its familiar configuration. Some other intelligence from another dimension was struggling to supersede human observation and transform this universe into its own framework!

Abruptly Dr. Edwards closed the paper, returned it to the shelf, and retrieved her jacket.

She had to know more. She had to find someone who could provide information.

She moved through the entryway to the door, emerged onto the walkway. Outside she looked skyward, trying to locate the sun. But there wasn't any sun—only an all-pervading grayness that shrouded everything—not a gray fog, but a gray emptiness that seemed devoid of life, of any movement.

The walkway led to the street and there it ended, but as she moved forward the pavement came into view and the building ahead loomed out of the gray, but a building with distortions.

She moved forward rapidly. Visibility extended only a few meters, and as she approached them the buildings materialized like two-dimensional projections without depth, like twisted cardboard structures appearing in misty conditions.

Once she stopped and looked back and saw that the grayness had closed in behind her. The buildings were erased, the walkway faded into nothing.

She called out, hoping to attract attention. But her voice frightened her. It seemed to echo upward into higher levels of the atmosphere, as if a giant opening had appeared to a vast space high above her.

She continued until she came to the corner of Maritime. There, on the curb, she stopped and stared. The gray barrier was thicker there, but she did not realize how close it was until she glanced down and saw there was nothing, nothing at all beyond the curb. No dull gleam of wet pavement, no sign of a street. It was as if all existence ended here at the corner of Harbor and Maritime.

With a sharp cry, Dr. Edwards turned and ran. Back down the street she raced, jacket streaming behind her in the wind. She felt the notebook bouncing in her pocket with each stride—that precious, irreplaceable record of her work.

Breathing hard, she reached her building and stumbled up the walkway, grateful that it still existed.

On the threshold she stood for a moment, catching her breath. She glanced back over her shoulder, and a strange feeling of inner emptiness seemed to wash over her. At that moment, the gray nothingness appeared to thin—the enveloping curtain fell away, and she saw...

Vague and indistinct, yet cast in holographic outline, an enormous structure was silhouetted against the darkening sky. It was a structure fantastic with geometric domes, crystalline towers, and suspended platforms and connecting bridges. Corridor-like passages, flanked on either side by luminous panels and transport systems, stretched endlessly to the vanishing point. Great beams of multicolored energy probed huge patterns and spirals above the higher levels.

And beyond, like a final backdrop, rose a colossal barrier. It was from that barrier—from its angular projections and geometric features—that Dr. Edwards felt the presence observing her.

Thousands of consciousnesses focused with a single purpose.

And as she continued to observe, something else seemed to form above that barrier. A pattern this time, that swirled and shifted in the ribbons of energy and rapidly coalesced into strange mathematical configurations, without definite form or detail. A vast intelligence, an intelligence of incomprehensible power and purpose, staring down with calculating composure.

Then the structure and the intelligence slid out of focus; the vision faded like a deactivated hologram, and the grayness returned.

Dr. Edwards pushed open the door of her apartment. But she did not lock it. There was no purpose in locks—not anymore.

The temperature control was still functioning, and she adjusted it upward, though she knew the cold she felt came from within.

Without removing her jacket, she sank exhausted into her chair, closed her eyes then opened them again.

She sighed with relief as she saw the room was unchanged. Everything in its accustomed place: the chronometer, the specimen jar, the equipment on the shelf, the reef photograph on the wall facing her.

Everything was as it should be. The chronometer measured the silence with its silent display; it advanced to the next minute and the equipment emitted its usual faint hum.

This was her room, she thought. Rooms acquire the identity of the person who inhabits them, become part of them. This was her world, her own private world, and as such it would be the last to go.

But how long could she—her consciousness—maintain its existence?

Dr. Edwards stared at the reef photograph, and for a moment a small measure of reassurance returned to her. The coral formations glowed with remembered color—the anemones, the schools of fish frozen in their dance, the distant submersible that had once carried her into those depths. They couldn't take this away. The rest of the world might dissolve because there was insufficient observational power to maintain its configuration.

But this room was hers. She alone had furnished it. She alone, since she had first moved into this apartment, had lived here.

This room would remain. It must remain—it must...

She rose from her chair and walked across the room to the bookshelf, stood staring at the second level with its single publication. Her eyes shifted to the top level, and swift terror gripped her.

For not all the books were there. Many books weren't there! Only the most familiar, the most frequently referenced ones.

So the transformation had already begun here! The unfamiliar books were gone, and that fit the pattern—for it would be the least familiar things that would disappear first.

Turning, she stared across the room. Was it her imagination, or did the specimen jar on the table blur and begin to fade?

But as she stared at it, it became clear again, a solid, substantial object.

For a moment real fear reached out and touched her with icy fingers. For she knew that this room no longer was protected against the thing that had happened out there on the street.

Or had it really happened? Might not all this exist within her own mind? Might not the street be as it always was, with researchers walking and equipment functioning? Might not the Blue Whale Café still exist, its blue neon sign glowing in the evening?

Could it be that she was losing her sanity? She had heard whispers when she had passed, whispers the gossiping researchers had not intended her to hear. And she had seen the looks when she walked by. They thought her unstable. Could she be actually unstable?

But she knew she wasn't unstable. She knew that she perhaps was the most rational of all people who walked the earth. For she, and she alone, had foreseen this very thing. And the others had dismissed her for it.

Somewhere else the researchers might be working in a laboratory. But it would be a different laboratory. And the researchers undoubtedly would be different too.

For the matter of which the laboratory and everything within it had been formed would now be cast in a different configuration, claimed by different consciousnesses in a different dimension.

"Perhaps we shall encounter a day, far distant, when our dimension, our world will dissolve beneath our feet and before our eyes as some stronger consciousness reaches out from the dimensional shadows of the very space we inhabit and wrests from us the matter which we know to be our own."

But there had been no need to wait for that distant day. Scant years after she had written those prophetic words, the thing was happening. Humanity had played unwittingly into the hands of those other consciousnesses in the other dimension. Humanity had waged wars, and wars had created conditions for mass disappearances. And the whole vast cycle of events was but a component of a strategic plan.

She could see it all now. By an insidious form of manipulation, entities from that other dimension—or was it one supreme intelligence—had deliberately created the conditions for conflict. The reduction of the world's consciousness had been carefully planned with calculated premeditation.

On impulse she suddenly turned, crossed the room, and opened the connecting door to the bedroom. She stopped on the threshold, and a sound of despair forced its way to her lips.

There was no bedroom. Where her bed and storage units had been, there was grayish nothingness. Her notebook—she had left it in the bedside drawer. It was gone now, claimed by the void along with everything else in that room.

Like an automaton, she turned again and moved to the entry door. Here, too, she found what she had expected. There was no entryway, no familiar jacket hook and equipment rack.

Nothing...

Weakly Dr. Edwards moved back to her chair in the corner.

"So here I am," she said, half aloud.

So there she was. Making a final stand in the last corner of the world that remained to her.

Perhaps there were other people like her, she thought. People who stood at bay against the emptiness that marked the transition from one dimension to another. People who had lived close to the things they valued, who had endowed those things with such substantial form by power of consciousness alone that they now stood out alone against the power of some greater consciousness.

The street was gone. The rest of her apartment was gone. This room still retained its form.

This room, she knew, would remain the longest. And when the rest of the room was gone, this corner with her chair would persist. For this was the location where she had lived for fifteen years. The bedroom was for sleeping, the kitchenette for eating. This room was for living. This was her final stand.

These were the walls and floors and photographs and equipment that had absorbed her will to make them walls and photographs and equipment.

She looked toward the window into a blank world. The adjacent buildings were already gone. Others had not lived with them as she had lived with this room. Their attention had been divided, broadly distributed; their thoughts had not been concentrated as hers upon an area five blocks by four, or a room fifteen by thirteen.

Staring toward the window, she saw it again. The same vision she had observed before, yet different in an indescribable way. There was the structure illuminated against the sky. There were the geometric towers and crystalline features, the dome-shaped projections and platforms. She could see with stereoscopic clarity the suspended bridges, the luminous corridors sweeping on into infinity. The vision was closer this time, but the depth and proportion had changed—as if she were viewing it from two concurrent perspectives simultaneously.

And the intelligence—the intelligence of magnitude—of power, of cosmic strategy and purpose...

Dr. Edwards turned her attention back into the room. The chronometer was advancing slowly, steadily. The grayness was infiltrating the room.

The desk and equipment were the first to go. They simply faded away, and with them went one corner of the room.

And then the specimen jar.

"Oh, well," said Dr. Edwards, "I never did value that particularly."

Now as she sat there, it didn't seem strange to be without the desk or the equipment. It was as if it were something quite normal. Something one could expect to happen.

Perhaps, if she concentrated hard enough, she could restore them.

But, after all, what was the purpose? One person, alone, could not resist the irresistible advance of nothingness. One person, all alone, simply couldn't do it.

She wondered what the specimen jar looked like in that other dimension. It certainly wouldn't be a specimen jar, nor would the equipment be equipment, for perhaps they didn't have specimen jars or equipment in the invading dimension.

She wondered, as a matter of fact, what she herself would look like when she finally transitioned into the unknown. For she was matter, too, just as the specimen jar and equipment were matter.

She wondered if she would retain her individuality—if she still would be a person. Or would she merely be a thing?

There was one answer to all of that. She simply didn't know.

Nothingness advanced upon her, consumed its way across the room, approaching her as she sat in the chair beneath the shelf. And she waited for it.

The room, or what remained of it, plunged into profound silence.

Dr. Edwards started. The chronometer had stopped. Strange—the first time in fifteen years.

She leaped from her chair and then sat down again.

The chronometer hadn't stopped.

It wasn't there.

She looked at the wall facing her. The reef photograph remained—the coral, the fish, the distant submersible. Of all the objects in the room, it alone persisted, suspended now in the encroaching grayness. The image she had looked at every evening for fifteen years, the one thing her consciousness had held most firmly in its grasp.

There was a tingling sensation in her feet.
problem_data.question: What object was most important to Dr. Edwards in her room?
problem_data.correct_answer: A framed photograph of a coral reef
answers: A framed photograph of a coral reef
